explanation: Fires on a token inside or right after an alphanumeric identifier, model number or citation number: page-range hyphens in journal citations (565-577), digits within product/model numbers, version numbers and reference IDs, and the word after a proper name in a name compound (Bombers[ Football] Club, Crytek[ Group]). Ordinary prose tokens barely activate it.

Fires on a word in mid-clause position, usually a noun or determiner that is the object of a verb or preposition (his[ comments], steer[ the], care of[ the], handing[ him]). It shows no clear dependence on topic or token identity, so strength is hard to predict.

Fires on the later pieces of acronyms and abbreviated organization/degree names (Check[ Point], B[PO], C[PO], MB Ch[M], EM[R], HP[SE]), and also on sentence-initial 'With' at the start of a new paragraph in news text. Weak on ordinary words.

Fires on structural or connective tokens in formulaic or technical text: the binary minus in auto-generated algebra problems ('u*i(r)[ -] 3*v(r)'), ternary '?', citation brackets/'#', separators in tables and file paths, and the next token in license or boilerplate templates. Weak in plain prose.

Fires on comparison and equality-test tokens in code: '==', '===', '!=', 'equals', assert/CHECK_EQUAL, isset, is_null, IfEmpty, 'not found/present', defined(). Strongest on test-assertion names and emptiness/existence checks, moderate on plain '==' inside if conditions.

Fires on the token that starts a declaration right after a code file's header, mostly 'public' before class/interface after Java imports or javadoc, and '{' after a C# namespace line. It also fires on some unrelated tokens, such as 'and[ so] on', 'third[ derivative]' and the word after list punctuation.

Fires on a wide, mixed set of tokens: 'bake[ for]', 'known[ as]', 'v. [STATE] of', acronyms in parentheses ('(AC)', '(CS)'), hyphens inside chemical names, and parts of compound words. None of these share an obvious feature.

Fires on the preposition or word right after a reporting/speech verb in news style ('said[ on] Monday', 'announced[ on]', 'said[ in] a statement', 'argued[ in]'). Also on 'type' in '<link rel=stylesheet type=' and 'to[ any] person' in MIT license text. The main use is the attribution phrase after a verb of saying.

Fires on array/list-type tokens and syntax in code: 'array' return types, '[]', 'Array', 'vector', 'Arrays.asList', Lisp quoted lists "'(", and the closing ')' after an isArray(...) call. Strongest where a token marks or creates an array or list type or value.

Fires on the word after a quantifier of plurality ('many/several/14[ different]', 'a number of[ different]', 'number of[ nodes/teams]', 'multi[-user]', 'Multi-[Channel]') and on 'a lot going[ on]'. Responds to the plural noun or adjective that a multiplicity word modifies.

Fires on the keyword right after a declaration modifier in code (CREATE OR REPLACE[ FUNCTION], CREATE[ TABLE], static[ class], 'function request(url,[ options]'). Separately, it fires on French negation 'ne/n'' and on fragments of technical or Latin words. Mostly a code-declaration-keyword unit with unrelated offshoots.

Fires on content words and word pieces in non-English Romance and Germanic prose (Spanish, French, Portuguese, Italian, German, some Russian), especially words inside fixed multiword phrases ('hacer[ frente]', 'au[ cours]', 'à la[ suite]', 'antes de'). Barely fires in English (only weakly on 'what').

Fires on a mixed set of tokens: the 'accelerate/accelerated/accelerating' word family, 'real[ estate]', '#define[ pb]', name fragments, and non-English function words. Only the accelerate family and 'real estate' form clear clusters.

Fires on words for persistence or continuation despite something, most strongly 'still' ('still remain', 'still holds', 'the problem stays'). Also on related words: cling, stubborn, hold/holding, remain, leave/left untouched, and 'but' that introduces a persisting fact.
